name: Painkiller
variant: Pusser's 4-1-1 spec, No. 2 strength (after the Soggy Dollar Bar original)
creator: Daphne Henderson
location: White Bay, Jost Van Dyke, British Virgin Islands

ingredients.orig: Pusser's Rum — 2 oz for a No. 2; No. 3 = 3 oz, No. 4 = 4 oz

glass: tall glass or Pusser's enamel tin mug
source: Pusser's Rum official recipe (4 parts pineapple, 1 cream of coconut, 1 orange, rum to taste by number); history via Wikipedia and Chilled Magazine
notes: Created by Daphne Henderson at a swim-up beach bar in the BVI. Pusser's founder Charles Tobias could not get her recipe and reportedly worked up his own match; the company trademarked the name in 1989, so the brand's 4:1:1 ratio with Pusser's is now the reference. It is ordered by number (No. 2, 3 or 4) for the ounces of rum; the No. 4 roughly doubles the strength. Basically a Piña Colada rounded out with orange juice and finished with a heavy nutmeg cap.

name: Piña Colada
variant: Caribe Hilton, 1954 (hotel's published recipe)
creator: Ramón 'Monchito' Marrero

ingredients.orig: coconut cream (sweetened cream of coconut, i.e. Coco López)

source: Caribe Hilton / Hilton Stories (hotel's own published recipe: blend with 1/2 cup crushed ice ~15 seconds)
notes: The hotel's own recipe splits the coconut between one part sweet cream of coconut and one part heavy cream, so it is richer and less sugary than most later bar specs, with a big 6 oz of pineapple. Marrero is said to have spent three months on it once canned cream of coconut made the drink practical; some accounts say it was first shaken rather than blended. Puerto Rico made it the official national drink in 1978.

name: Piña Colada
variant: Barrachina, Old San Juan, 1963 (house frozen-base method)
creator: Ramón Portas Mingot

ingredients.orig: rum, a shot poured into the glass first ('to taste')
1 part Coco López or Goya cream of coconut
3/4 part water blended into the base (batch: 48 oz pineapple, 15 oz coconut cream, 10 oz water)

source: Barrachina's house method as reported by The Kitchn (bartender interview) and The Georgetowner (restaurant's batch recipe)
notes: The rival birthplace claim: a plaque at Barrachina credits Mingot with the drink in 1963. Their base is pineapple and cream of coconut at about 4:1, thinned with water and frozen to a slush without ice. Rum goes into the glass first and the slush is poured over it, and there's no dairy. Some retellings say Mingot's first version used condensed milk, but the restaurant's current method doesn't.

name: Piña Colada
variant: IBA official specification
source: International Bartenders Association official cocktail list (recalled; the IBA page was not reachable this session)
notes: The IBA version is much drier and stronger than the Caribe Hilton original: pineapple only matches the rum, and there's no heavy cream. It is the standard spec in bartending courses and international hotel bars, and a useful low-juice reference point for the colada family.

name: Hurricane
variant: Pat O'Brien's 1940s original (Jeff Berry's reconstruction)
source: Jeff Berry, Beachbum Berry Remixed (2010), as quoted by Moody Mixologist and others
notes: Invented to clear out cases of unpopular rum the bar was made to buy before its distributor would sell it whiskey. The pre-mix drink was just rum, lemon and passion-fruit syrup at 4:2:2, which amounts to an oversized passion-fruit sour on dark rum. Nobody wrote the original down; Berry's 4:2:2 is the accepted reconstruction.

name: Hurricane
variant: Smuggler's Cove craft spec (Martin Cate)
creator: Martin Cate (restoration of the 1940s formula)
garnish: cocktail umbrella speared into a lemon wedge
source: Martin & Rebecca Cate, Smuggler's Cove (2016)
notes: Cate keeps the three-ingredient 4:2:2 structure but uses molasses-heavy black blended rum and flash-blends it with 12 oz crushed ice plus a few agitator cubes. This is the fresh-ingredient Hurricane craft tiki bars point to when they reject the red mix.

name: Hurricane
variant: Modern two-rum fresh-juice version (as widely published, e.g. Liquor.com)
source: Liquor.com 'Hurricane' (fresh-ingredient version); the 2/2/2/1 core is repeated by many recipe sites. Lime/simple/grenadine amounts recalled, not re-verified
notes: The version most people now make from scratch. Passion fruit comes from juice or nectar rather than syrup, and orange juice and grenadine rebuild the fruitiness and red color the bottled mix gave. It is much juicier and less tart than the 1940s formula. Published amounts vary a lot (orange 1–2 oz, lime 0.5–1 oz).

name: Hurricane
variant: Pat O'Brien's today: 4 oz amber rum + 4 oz house Hurricane mix (mix mapped to real ingredients)

ingredients.orig: part of 4 oz Pat O'Brien's Hurricane Mix (red passion-fruit punch mix) — mapped
part of Hurricane Mix (citric tartness) — mapped
part of Hurricane Mix (red color, cherry-like sweetness) — mapped

glass: large (24 oz) Pat O'Brien's hurricane glass
source: Pat O'Brien's house spec (equal parts amber rum and Hurricane mix over cracked ice) as reported by Country Roads Magazine, Edible Times and Liquor & Drink; the breakdown of the mix is our own approximation
notes: What the courtyard bar actually pours: equal parts amber rum and its own red passion-fruit mix over cracked ice, a shortcut adopted once demand outgrew hand-squeezing. Critics call it 'red-flavored'. The mix is modeled here as sweetened passion-fruit nectar with a little lemon and grenadine, so the proportions are approximate, but the 1:1 rum-to-mix structure (4 oz rum) is documented.

name: Rum Runner
variant: Holiday Isle Tiki Bar, 1972 (Tiki John Ebert; as documented by Jeff Berry)
creator: John 'Tiki John' Ebert
source: Jeff Berry, Beachbum Berry Remixed (2010), p. 56; cross-checked against ultimatemaitai.com 'Perfect Pour Rum Runner' and Food.com 'Holiday Isle Rum Runner' (same fractions)
notes: Ebert made it to use up surplus blackberry brandy, banana liqueur and rum, and named it after the Keys' Prohibition smugglers. The documented original has no pineapple or orange juice. It is a blended, sweet-tart 151 sour where the two fruit liqueurs supply most of the sugar and flavor. One Holiday Isle-attributed variant splits the rum into 1/2 oz Bacardi Black plus 1/2 oz 151. Some sources date it to the 1950s.

name: Rum Runner
variant: Modern beach-bar version with pineapple (Difford's Guide spec)
source: Difford's Guide 'Rum Runner' (as summarized in search results; page not directly fetchable)
notes: On beach-bar menus the drink picked up pineapple (often orange as well) and standard-proof rums, with the 151 moved to an optional float and the grenadine sometimes floated for a sunset effect. Difford's version keeps it balanced with a full ounce of lime and uses more banana than blackberry. Keys bars still serve it either shaken or frozen.

name: Bahama Mama
variant: Classic bar-guide spec with coffee liqueur
source: Gary Regan, The Bartender's Bible (1991) / Webtender spec (recalled; not re-verified online this session)
notes: The older printed Bahama Mama is a long pineapple drink with three small rum pours (dark, coconut, 151) and a quarter-ounce of coffee liqueur, which adds a faint roasted note under the fruit. The Bahamian origin story is folklore; the drink spread through cruise ships and resort bars.

name: Bahama Mama
variant: Modern cruise/resort version (coconut rum, orange, grenadine)
source: Composite of common cruise-line and chain-restaurant specs (recalled; not verified this session)
notes: The Bahama Mama most vacationers are served drops the coffee liqueur and 151. It is coconut rum and dark rum stretched with equal pineapple and orange and tinted with grenadine, with no fresh citrus at all, so sweetness depends entirely on the juices. Representative proportions only; this is a composite of common specs.

name: Blue Hawaiian
variant: Blended resort version
source: Liquor.com 'Blue Hawaiian' (recalled; not re-verified online this session)
notes: Not to be confused with Harry Yee's Blue Hawaii (1957, sweet-and-sour, no coconut). The Blue Hawaiian crosses that drink with the Piña Colada and is effectively a blue colada. The curaçao adds orange-peel sweetness and color, which pushes the pineapple ratio lower than in a standard colada.

name: Lava Flow
variant: Hawaiian resort style

ingredients.orig: 2 oz strawberries, muddled with the rums

source: Liquor.com 'Lava Flow' (recalled; not re-verified online this session)
notes: The strawberries are muddled with the rums and poured into the glass first. A banana-pineapple-coconut blend goes in on top, so red streaks push up through the white like lava. Underneath the show it is a banana Piña Colada with a strawberry base; a fixture of Hawaiian hotel bars and luaus.

name: Chi Chi
variant: Vodka colada (common bar-guide spec)
source: Common bar-guide spec (e.g. The Bartender's Bible / Webtender); recalled, not re-verified this session
notes: A Piña Colada made with vodka, popular in Hawaiian hotel bars. With a neutral spirit, pineapple and coconut carry all the flavor. Published specs cluster around 1.5 oz vodka, 1–2 oz cream of coconut and 3–4 oz pineapple.

name: Yellow Bird
variant: Caribbean resort version (rum, Galliano, banana, orange, pineapple)
source: Composite of commonly published Caribbean resort specs (recalled; not verified this session)
notes: Named for the Caribbean song 'Yellow Bird', a hit for Arthur Lyman in 1961. The resort version sets Galliano's vanilla-anise and banana liqueur over orange and pineapple, and the result really is yellow. A separate, shorter 'Yellow Bird' sour (rum, Galliano, triple sec, lime) also exists in bar guides and is not this drink.

name: Goombay Smash
variant: Copycat of Miss Emily's Blue Bee Bar recipe (the original is a family secret)
creator: Emily Cooper ('Miss Emily')
location: New Plymouth, Green Turtle Cay, Abaco, Bahamas
source: Common copycat recipes of the Blue Bee Bar drink (recalled; not verified this session)
notes: The signature of a tiny Out Island bar, sold by the jug, with the formula kept in the family. Copycats agree on coconut rum, a second darker rum, a little apricot brandy and a lot of pineapple. Treat the proportions as a reconstruction.

name: Bushwacker
variant: Blended (standard modern spec)
source: Liquor.com 'Bushwacker' spec (recalled; not re-verified online this session)
notes: A boozy coconut milkshake: coffee and chocolate liqueurs over cream of coconut and milk, blended with dark rum. It started in the Virgin Islands in the mid-1970s and became the house drink of Florida Panhandle beach bars (Pensacola Beach, Flora-Bama). Gulf Coast versions often add a 151 float or ice cream.

name: Miami Vice
variant: Frozen Piña Colada and frozen Strawberry Daiquiri poured side by side

ingredients.orig: light rum, 1.5 oz in each half

source: Composite of common published specs (recalled; not verified this session)
notes: Named after the 1980s TV show. Two frozen drinks, a Strawberry Daiquiri and a Piña Colada, are blended separately and poured together, layered or swirled, so the tart strawberry half and the rich coconut half mix as you drink. A cruise-ship and beach-bar staple.

name: Strawberry Daiquiri
variant: Frozen, blended with fresh strawberries
source: Representative of common published specs (e.g. Liquor.com, Difford's); recalled, not re-verified this session
notes: The blender-era daiquiri that made rum sours a mass-market vacation drink. Fresh berries add body and sugar, so the syrup can come down slightly from a classic daiquiri. Resort bars usually swap the berries for sweetened strawberry purée or mix, which makes it much sweeter.

name: Banana Daiquiri
variant: Frozen resort style (St. Thomas tradition)
source: Composite of common resort specs (recalled; not verified this session)
notes: A whole ripe banana turns the frozen daiquiri thick and custardy, and a little banana liqueur backs it up. The Mountain Top lookout on St. Thomas advertises itself as the home of the original. Proportions here are representative, not a documented house spec.

name: Dirty Banana
variant: Jamaican resort version
source: Composite of common Jamaican resort specs (recalled; not verified this session)
notes: The favorite blended drink of Jamaica's all-inclusive resorts, built on two island exports, gold rum and Tia Maria, blended with ripe banana and milk. Many bars add banana liqueur, cream or ice cream. With no citrus at all it belongs with the creamy coladas, not the sours.

name: Jamaican Rum Punch
variant: Resort/home style: overproof rum and strawberry syrup ('one sour, two sweet, three strong, four weak')
source: Composite of common Jamaican rum-punch recipes following the traditional rhyme (recalled; not verified this session)
notes: Jamaica's everyday punch follows the old 1-2-3-4 rhyme but uses the island's own ingredients: raw 63% white overproof for 'strong', bright red strawberry syrup for 'sweet', and fruit juices for 'weak'. It is sweeter and far more estery than the Bajan version. Recorded in rhyme parts as ounces, making two servings.

name: Bajan Rum Punch
variant: Barbados, 'one of sour, two of sweet, three of strong, four of weak'
source: Traditional Barbadian proportion rhyme, as served in Bajan hotels and rum shops (recalled; not verified this session)
notes: The Barbados form of the Caribbean punch rhyme is plain water, not juice, for the 'weak', finished with Angostura and nutmeg. That makes it a drier, rum-forward punch that shows off Bajan rum. Recorded in rhyme parts as ounces, making two servings; the 'water' ID is proposed in resort.new-ingredients.json.

name: Mai Tai
variant: Hawaiian resort style (pineapple and orange juice with a dark-rum float)
source: Composite of Hawaiian hotel-bar specs (recalled; not verified this session)
notes: The Mai Tai as served poolside across Hawaii descends from the Royal Hawaiian's 1953 pineapple-and-orange version. Light rum is stretched with juice, lightly sweetened with orgeat and curaçao, and capped with a dark-rum float so the first sips taste strong. Structurally it is a juice-forward resort punch, not the short 1944 sour, which is why it sits in resort-punch with mai-tai as a secondary family.

name: Malibu Bay Breeze
variant: Malibu brand spec
source: Malibu brand recipe (recalled; not re-verified online this session)
notes: Malibu's coconut-rum version of the vodka Bay Breeze, from the Sea Breeze family of 1980s highballs. It is the simplest resort tropical: sweet coconut liqueur, pineapple and tart cranberry built over ice, with no added citrus or syrup.

name: Planter's Punch
variant: Myers's rum bottle-label recipe
creator: Fred L. Myers & Son (brand recipe)
source: Myers's Rum back-label / brand recipe (recalled; not re-verified online this session)
notes: The version millions learned from the Myers's bottle. Orange juice does most of the work, so it is much softer and less tart than the 'one of sour' Jamaican formula, with grenadine only for color. It was the de facto resort Planter's Punch for decades and is distinct from the lime-and-sugar ancestor recorded in the ancestors slice.

name: Zombie
variant: Mid-century bar-guide / chain-restaurant style (apricot brandy, pineapple, orange, 151 float)

ingredients.orig: orange juice (some guides use papaya juice)

source: Representative of mid-century bar guides such as Mr. Boston (recalled; exact spec not re-verified this session)
notes: Before Jeff Berry decoded Don's formula, most drinkers got this bar-guide Zombie: no Don's Mix, falernum or Pernod. Apricot brandy and fruit juice stand in for the secret spice, and a 151 float keeps the drink's knockout reputation. Its descendants still appear on chain and resort menus.

name: Scorpion Bowl
variant: New England Chinese-restaurant (Polynesian-Chinese) bowl
venue: Polynesian-Chinese restaurants (e.g. Hong Kong, Harvard Square; Kowloon, Saugus)

ingredients.orig: 151 poured into the center 'volcano' well and set alight

glass: ceramic scorpion bowl with center volcano well, long straws
source: Composite of Boston-area restaurant descriptions and home recreations (recalled; not verified this session)
notes: Trader Vic's shareable Scorpion as it survived in New England's Polynesian-Chinese restaurants: a big ceramic bowl of rum, a splash of gin or vodka and brandy, orange juice and almond syrup, with a flaming 151 volcano in the middle and a straw for each person. The house versions are usually premixed and sweeter than Vic's. Treat the proportions as representative.
